summary.text: At each prime-power level, the proof organizes the elements into laminar orbits of residues up to sign and colors them so that opposite non-self-opposite residues have opposite colors; weighting these families by \(\log p\), a Hall matching and quadratic-form argument using the conditional negative definiteness of \(\log(x+y)\) and \(|x-y|<x+y\) yields \(|A|\le 3r^2+2\), where \(r\) is the number of relevant primes. Hence extremality gives \(f(n)\ge \sqrt{(n-2)/3}\), and therefore \(f(n)/\log n\to\infty\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 \Pi(A)=\prod_{(a,b)\in A^2,\ a\ne b}(a+b),\qquad
 P(A)=|\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p\mid \Pi(A)\}|.
\]
The product is over ordered pairs, but of course this does not affect its set of prime divisors. We shall prove the stronger uniform estimate
\[
                         |A|\le 3P(A)^2+2.                 \tag{1}
\]
The asserted limit will follow readily.

We first develop the ingredients needed for (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. A two-coloring attached to each prime
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For a prime p and a positive integer x, write
\[
 x=p^{\nu_p(x)}u_p(x),\qquad p\nmid u_p(x).
\]
Define a color \(\chi_p(x)\in\{0,1\}\) as follows. If p is odd, color x according as the least positive residue of \(u_p(x)\pmod p\) lies in the lower or upper half of the nonzero residues; concretely, one may put
\[
 \chi_p(x)=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 2(u_p(x)\bmod p)<p.
\]
For p=2, use the odd part modulo 4 instead:
\[
 \chi_2(x)=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 2(u_2(x)\bmod 4)<4.
\]
Thus the two odd residue classes 1 and 3 modulo 4 receive different colors.

The essential coloring property is
\[
 \chi_p(a)=\chi_p(b)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \nu_p(a+b)\le \nu_p(2a)                         \tag{2}
\]
for all positive a,b.

To prove this, suppose instead that \(\nu_p(a+b)>\nu_p(2a)\). In particular,
\(\nu_p(a+b)>\nu_p(a)\). The elementary valuation rule then forces
\(\nu_p(a)=\nu_p(b)\): indeed, if one of these two valuations were smaller, the
valuation of their sum would equal the smaller one. Put this common valuation
equal to e and cancel \(p^e\).

If p is odd, the resulting p-free parts satisfy
\[
 u_p(a)+u_p(b)\equiv0\pmod p.
\]
Their nonzero residues are negatives of one another. Since p is odd, neither
can be the midpoint p/2, and two opposite nonzero residues lie in different
halves of \([0,p)\). Hence their colors differ, a contradiction.

If p=2, our assumption says
\(\nu_2(a+b)>\nu_2(2a)=e+1\). After canceling \(2^e\), it follows that
\[
 u_2(a)+u_2(b)\equiv0\pmod4.
\]
Both parts are odd, so their residues modulo 4 are 1 and 3 in some order, and
again their colors differ. This proves (2).

An immediate useful reformulation is the following. For every \(k\ge0\),
\[
 \begin{split}
 &p^{k+1}\mid a+b,\qquad p^{k+1}\nmid2a\\
 &\hspace{35mm}\Longrightarrow\quad \chi_p(a)\ne\chi_p(b). \tag{3}
 \end{split}
\]
Indeed, equal colors would give by (2)
\(\nu_p(a+b)\le\nu_p(2a)\), contrary to the two divisibility conditions.

For completeness, this coloring already gives the weaker bound
\(|A\setminus\{0\}|\le2^{P(A)}\): associate to each positive a the vector
\((\chi_p(a))_{p\mid\Pi(A)}\). If two distinct positive a,b had the same
vector, (2), for every prime dividing a+b, would imply \(a+b\mid2a\). Reversing
a and b gives \(a+b\mid2b\). Hence \(a+b\le2a\) and \(a+b\le2b\), forcing
b\(\le a\) and a\(\le b\), a contradiction. We need a stronger, quadratic
argument below.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Negation orbits and laminar families
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let V be a finite set of vertices, and let \(v:V\to G\), where G is a finite
abelian group. For \(i\in V\), define its negation orbit
\[
 O_v(i)=\{j\in V:v(j)=v(i)\text{ or }v(j)=-v(i)\}.
\]
Two such orbits are either disjoint or equal. Call an orbit mixed if it contains
both a value x and its negative \(-x\), with \(x\ne-x\). Every mixed orbit has
at least two vertices. Let \({\cal F}(v)\) be the family of distinct mixed
orbits.

Suppose in addition that \(\sigma:V\to\{0,1\}\) has the separation property
\[
 v(i)=-v(j),\quad v(i)\ne-v(i)
       \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma(i)\ne\sigma(j).       \tag{4}
\]
Inside a mixed orbit, vertices with equal v-values have equal colors, and
vertices with opposite v-values have opposite colors. To see the first claim,
choose in the mixed orbit a vertex k whose value is opposite to their common
value. Both vertices have color different from \(\sigma(k)\), and because there
are only two colors their colors agree. The second claim is exactly (4).
Consequently, for i,j the number of mixed orbits containing both is at most
one, and more precisely
\[
 \sum_{U\in{\cal F}(v)}1_{i,j\in U,\ \sigma(i)\ne\sigma(j)}
 =1_{v(i)=-v(j),\ v(i)\ne-v(i)},                         \tag{5}
\]
while
\[
 \sum_{U\in{\cal F}(v)}1_{i,j\in U,\ \sigma(i)=\sigma(j)}
 \le1_{v(i)=v(j),\ v(i)\ne-v(i)}.                       \tag{6}
\]

We apply this with
\[
 G=\mathbb Z/p^{k+1}\mathbb Z,\qquad v_{p,k}(i)=a_i\pmod {p^{k+1}},
                                                               \tag{7}
\]
where the \(a_i\)'s are positive integers. By (3), the fixed coloring
\(\sigma(i)=\chi_p(a_i)\) satisfies (4) at every level k. Notice also that
reduction modulo a lower power sends a negation orbit at a higher level into a
negation orbit at the lower level. It follows that the collection of all mixed
orbits over levels \(0\le k<K\) is laminar: two members are either disjoint, or
one contains the other. At the same level they are disjoint or equal; at
different levels, reduce the finer congruence modulo the coarser modulus.

For a fixed p and cutoff K, define a kernel
\[
 M_p(i,j)=\log p\sum_{0\le k<K}\sum_{U\in{\cal F}(v_{p,k})}1_{i,j\in U}. \tag{8}
\]
Thus \(M_p\) is the weighted co-membership kernel of a laminar family, every
member of which has at least two vertices. It has nonnegative entries and is
symmetric. It is also positive semidefinite, because for every real vector z,
\[
 \sum_{i,j}z_i z_jM_p(i,j)
 =\log p\sum_{k<K}\sum_{U\in{\cal F}(v_{p,k})}
            \left(\sum_{i\in U}z_i\right)^2\ge0.             \tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. An abstract signed laminar-kernel bound
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now prove the kernel inequality which is responsible for the quadratic
bound. Let V have n vertices, with \(n\ge2\), and let \({\cal P}\) be an index
set of size r. For each \(p\in{\cal P}\), let \(M_p\) be a nonnegative weighted
co-membership kernel of a laminar family of subsets of V, all of size at least
two. Give every vertex a color \(\sigma_p(i)\in\{0,1\}\), and set
\[
 C(i,j)=\sum_{p:\,\sigma_p(i)\ne\sigma_p(j)}M_p(i,j),\qquad
 R(i,j)=\sum_{p:\,\sigma_p(i)=\sigma_p(j)}M_p(i,j).          \tag{10}
\]
Assume:

(i) C is conditionally negative semidefinite, meaning
\[
 \sum_{i,j}z_i z_jC(i,j)\le0\quad\text{whenever }\sum_i z_i=0; \tag{11}
\]

(ii) for every \(i\ne j\),
\[
                         R(i,j)<C(i,j).                       \tag{12}
\]

We claim that
\[
                             n\le3r^2.                         \tag{13}
\]

Write
\[
 S=\sum_{i,j}C(i,j),\qquad T=\sum_p\sum_iM_p(i,i).            \tag{14}
\]
There are two complementary budget inequalities:
\[
                         S\le rT,                              \tag{15}
\]
\[
                         nT\le3rS.                             \tag{16}
\]
We prove each in full.

First associate to a Boolean color its sign \(\varepsilon_p(i)\in\{1,-1\}\),
and define
\[
 Q(i,j)=\sum_p\varepsilon_p(i)\varepsilon_p(j)M_p(i,j)
       =R(i,j)-C(i,j).                                        \tag{17}
\]
Each signed kernel
\(Q_p(i,j)=\varepsilon_p(i)\varepsilon_p(j)M_p(i,j)\) is positive
semidefinite: its quadratic form at z is that of \(M_p\) at the vector
\((\varepsilon_p(i)z_i)_i\). Hence Q, their sum, is positive semidefinite.
Also \(Q(i,j)<0\) off the diagonal by (12), and
\[
 \sum_iQ(i,i)=T.                                              \tag{18}
\]

For any sign vector s, expansion and the nonpositivity of the off-diagonal
entries give
\[
 q_Q(s)+q_Q(\mathbf1)
 =\sum_{i,j}(s_i s_j+1)Q(i,j)\le2\sum_iQ(i,i)=2T.             \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, on the diagonal the coefficient is 2, while off the diagonal it is
either 0 or 2, hence is nonnegative and multiplies a nonpositive number.
For a fixed p, take \(s_i=\varepsilon_p(i)\). Then
\[
 q_{Q_p}(s)=\sum_{i,j}M_p(i,j).
\]
Since \(Q-Q_p\) is positive semidefinite,
\[
 \sum_{i,j}M_p(i,j)\le q_Q(s)\le2T,
\]
the last inequality using (19) and \(q_Q(\mathbf1)\ge0\). Summing this over p
gives
\[
 \sum_{p,i,j}M_p(i,j)\le2rT.                                 \tag{20}
\]
On the other hand, (10) and (17) give pointwise
\[
 \sum_pM_p(i,j)=2C(i,j)+Q(i,j).
\]
After summing, and again using \(q_Q(\mathbf1)\ge0\), (20) yields
\(2S\le2rT\), proving (15).

We next prove (16). We need a matching fact about a laminar family. Given one
of our laminar families, for every vertex i choose a smallest family member
containing i; if no member contains i, choose all of V. Call the resulting set
\(A_i\). Then \(i\in A_i\), \(|A_i|\ge2\), and the \(A_i\)'s are laminar.
Moreover, every original family member containing i contains \(A_i\).

There is an injection
\[
 H:V\longrightarrow V\times\{0,1\}                           \tag{21}
\]
such that, writing \(h(i)\) for the first coordinate of H(i),
\[
 h(i)\in A_i\setminus\{i\}.                                  \tag{22}
\]
Here is a proof using Hall's theorem. For \(X\subseteq V\), put
\[
 N(X)=\bigcup_{i\in X}(A_i\setminus\{i\}).
\]
Let \(B=X\setminus N(X)\). Distinct i,j in B must have disjoint \(A_i,A_j\):
if, say, \(A_i\subseteq A_j\), then \(i\in A_j\setminus\{j\}\subseteq N(X)\),
contrary to \(i\in B\), and similarly for the reverse inclusion. Choose one
element \(g(i)\in A_i\setminus\{i\}\) for each i. For i in B these chosen
elements are distinct, by disjointness, and all lie in N(X). Thus
\(|B|\le|N(X)|\). Also \(|X\cap N(X)|\le|N(X)|\), so
\[
 |X|\le2|N(X)|=|N(X)\times\{0,1\}|.
\]
This is precisely Hall's condition for matching i into two copies of
\(A_i\setminus\{i\}\), proving (21)-(22).

Because every family member containing i also contains h(i), co-membership is
preserved:
\[
                         M_p(i,h(i))=M_p(i,i).                 \tag{23}
\]
Furthermore, for any p and distinct i,j,
\[
                         M_p(i,j)\le C(i,j).                   \tag{24}
\]
If the p-colors differ, \(M_p(i,j)\) is one of the nonnegative summands in C.
If they agree, it is a summand of R, so
\(M_p(i,j)\le R(i,j)<C(i,j)\).
Combining (22)-(24),
\[
                         M_p(i,i)\le C(i,h(i)).                \tag{25}
\]

It remains to exploit conditional negative semidefiniteness. The kernel C is
symmetric and has zero diagonal. Put
\[
 \rho_i=\sum_jC(i,j),\qquad
 H_i=2n\rho_i-S.                                               \tag{26}
\]
Testing (11) on the zero-sum vector \(ne_i-\mathbf1\) gives \(H_i\ge0\).
Testing it on \(n(e_i+e_j)-2\mathbf1\), and expanding, gives
\[
                         n^2C(i,j)\le H_i+H_j.                 \tag{27}
\]
Also direct summation of (26) gives
\[
                         \sum_iH_i=nS.                         \tag{28}
\]
Multiply (25) by \(n^2\), use (27), and sum over i:
\[
 n^2\sum_iM_p(i,i)
 \le\sum_i(H_i+H_{h(i)}).
\]
Because H maps injectively into two copies of V and every \(H_j\ge0\), each
\(H_j\) is charged at most twice by the second sum. Therefore
\[
 \sum_iH_{h(i)}\le2\sum_iH_i,
\]
and by (28)
\[
 n^2\sum_iM_p(i,i)\le3nS.
\]
Dividing by n and summing over the r choices of p proves (16).

Finally, S is strictly positive. Choose \(i\ne j\). Since R has nonnegative
entries, (12) gives \(C(i,j)>0\), while all entries of C are nonnegative.
Now (15) and (16) imply
\[
 nS\le nrT=r(nT)\le3r^2S.
\]
Dividing by \(S>0\) proves (13).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Conditional negative definiteness of the logarithmic kernel
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We shall use the fact that on positive real numbers the kernel
\(L(x,y)=\log(x+y)\) is conditionally negative semidefinite.

Here is a proof. For x>0 put
\[
                         \phi(x)=\frac{x-1}{x+1}.
\]
Then \(|\phi(x)|<1\), and direct algebra gives
\[
 \log(x+y)=\log(x+1)+\log(y+1)-\log2
             +\log(1-\phi(x)\phi(y)).                         \tag{29}
\]
If \(\sum_i z_i=0\), the first three terms on the right, being a sum of a
function of i and a function of j, contribute zero to
\(\sum_{i,j}z_i z_jL(x_i,x_j)\). For the last term use
\[
 -\log(1-t)=\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{t^m}{m},\qquad |t|<1.
\]
It follows that
\[
 -\sum_{i,j}z_i z_j\log(1-\phi(x_i)\phi(x_j))
 =\sum_{m\ge1}\frac1m
       \left(\sum_i z_i\phi(x_i)^m\right)^2\ge0.              \tag{30}
\]
Thus
\[
 \sum_{i,j}z_i z_j\log(x_i+x_j)\le0,                          \tag{31}
\]
as claimed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Applying the kernels to pair sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(a:V\to\mathbb N_{>0}\) be injective, let \(n=|V|\ge2\), and let S be a
finite set of primes containing every prime divisor of \(a_i+a_j\) whenever
\(i\ne j\). Put \(r=|S|\). We prove
\[
                              n\le3r^2.                        \tag{32}
\]

Choose K so large that
\[
 \nu_p(a_i+a_j)\le K
 \quad\text{for every }p\in S\text{ and every }i,j\in V.      \tag{33}
\]
This is possible because all sets involved are finite. For each \(p\in S\),
use the laminar kernel \(M_p\) from (8) and color vertex i by \(\chi_p(a_i)\).
Define C and R by (10).

There is one harmless contribution not represented by mixed orbits. At level
(p,k), define the baseline kernel
\[
 D_{p,k}(i,j)=1_{v_{p,k}(i)=v_{p,k}(j),\ v_{p,k}(i)=-v_{p,k}(i)},
\]
and put
\[
 B(i,j)=\sum_{p\in S}\log p\sum_{k<K}D_{p,k}(i,j).             \tag{34}
\]
The baseline B is positive semidefinite. Indeed, for fixed p,k, group the
vertices by self-opposite residue classes x satisfying x=-x. Then
\[
 \sum_{i,j}z_i z_jD_{p,k}(i,j)
 =\sum_{x=-x}\left(\sum_{i:v_{p,k}(i)=x}z_i\right)^2\ge0.      \tag{35}
\]
Summing with the nonnegative weights \(\log p\) preserves this property.

For an integer m define the truncated prime-power count
\[
 N_{p,K}(m)=\#\{0\le k<K:p^{k+1}\mid m\}
           =\min(K,\nu_p(m))                                  \tag{36}
\]
when \(m>0\). Equations (5) and (6), together with the baseline, yield the two
fundamental entry relations
\[
 C(i,j)+B(i,j)
 =\sum_{p\in S}\log p\,N_{p,K}(a_i+a_j),                      \tag{37}
\]
and, for \(i\ne j\),
\[
 R(i,j)+B(i,j)
 \le\sum_{p\in S}\log p\,N_{p,K}(|a_i-a_j|).                 \tag{38}
\]
Let us explain exactly why. At a given level, a residue opposite to the other
residue is either non-self-opposite, in which case it lies in a mixed orbit and
the colors differ by (3), or self-opposite, in which case the baseline records
it. These mutually exclusive alternatives together say precisely that
\(p^{k+1}\mid a_i+a_j\), proving (37). Similarly, an equal residue is either
non-self-opposite and accounted for by a same-color mixed orbit, or is
self-opposite and accounted for by the baseline. This gives at most the
indicator of \(p^{k+1}\mid |a_i-a_j|\), proving (38). The inequality rather
than equality allows for the possibility that the relevant equal-residue
orbit is not mixed.

We also use the standard logarithmic factorization identity
\[
                         \log m=\sum_p\nu_p(m)\log p.          \tag{39}
\]
By (33), and because S contains the full prime support of every off-diagonal
sum, (37) gives for \(i\ne j\)
\[
                         C(i,j)+B(i,j)=\log(a_i+a_j).          \tag{40}
\]
On the diagonal, C(i,i)=0 and the baseline only counts some prime powers of
\(2a_i\), so
\[
                         B(i,i)\le\log(2a_i).                 \tag{41}
\]
For a difference, S need not contain all prime factors and K may truncate
valuations, but all omitted terms in (39) are nonnegative. Hence (38) gives
\[
                         R(i,j)+B(i,j)\le\log|a_i-a_j|         \tag{42}
\]
for \(i\ne j\).

We verify the two assumptions of the abstract bound. First, C is conditionally
negative semidefinite. If \(\sum_i z_i=0\), then (40), and (41) on the diagonal
(where the coefficient is \(z_i^2\ge0\)), imply
\[
 q_C(z)+q_B(z)
 \le\sum_{i,j}z_i z_j\log(a_i+a_j)\le0                       \tag{43}
\]
by (31). Since B is positive semidefinite, \(q_B(z)\ge0\), and therefore
\(q_C(z)\le0\).

Second, if \(i\ne j\), positivity and injectivity give
\[
 0<|a_i-a_j|<a_i+a_j.
\]
The logarithm is strictly increasing, so by (40) and (42),
\[
 R(i,j)+B(i,j)\le\log|a_i-a_j|
 <\log(a_i+a_j)=C(i,j)+B(i,j).
\]
Canceling B gives \(R(i,j)<C(i,j)\). All hypotheses of the abstract signed
laminar-kernel bound are now satisfied, proving (32).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The quadratic bound for an arbitrary set
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let A be any finite subset of the nonnegative integers and put
\[
 S=\{p:p\mid\Pi(A)\}.
\]
Every factor \(a+b\) belonging to an off-diagonal pair is positive, even if
one member is zero, so \(\Pi(A)\ne0\), and S consists of primes. Every prime
dividing a sum of two distinct members of A belongs to S.

Apply (32) to the positive members \(A\setminus\{0\}\), indexed injectively by
their values. If this set has at least two members, then
\[
 |A\setminus\{0\}|\le3|S|^2=3P(A)^2.
\]
Since deleting zero removes at most one member,
\(|A|\le3P(A)^2+1\), which is slightly stronger than needed in this case. If
\(|A\setminus\{0\}|<2\), then \(|A|\le2\). Thus in all cases
\[
                         |A|\le3P(A)^2+2,
\]
which proves (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Passage to the extremal function and the limit
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For each n, the values P(A) with \(|A|=n\) form a nonempty set of natural
numbers (for instance take \(A=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}\)), so they have an attained
minimum. The “greatest universal lower bound” in the definition of f is
exactly this minimum. Indeed, the minimum is a lower bound for all P(A), and
any universal lower bound is no larger than its value on a minimizing set.
Consequently, for every n there is an A with
\[
                         |A|=n,\qquad P(A)=f(n).               \tag{44}
\]

We show a uniform estimate strong enough for the desired limit. Fix any real
constant C. Since
\[
                         \frac{(\log x)^2}{x}\longrightarrow0,

a sufficiently large integer N satisfies, for every \(n\ge N\),
\[
                         3(C\log n)^2<n-2.                    \tag{45}
\]
We may also require \(N\ge3\). If A has \(|A|=n\ge N\), (1) gives
\[
                         n-2\le3P(A)^2.                       \tag{46}
\]
Together, (45)-(46) imply \(|C\log n|<P(A)\), unless C=0 where the desired
inequality is immediate. In every case,
\[
                         C\log n\le P(A).                     \tag{47}
\]
(The assertion is also automatic for negative C because \(\log n>0\) and
\(P(A)\ge0\).)

Choose in (47) a minimizing A as in (44). We obtain, for every \(n\ge N\),
\[
                         C\log n\le f(n).
\]
As \(n\ge3\), \(\log n>0\), and division gives
\[
                         C\le\frac{f(n)}{\log n}.             \tag{48}
\]
For every real C, inequality (48) holds eventually. This is precisely the
definition that
\[
                         \frac{f(n)}{\log n}\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
Since the argument applies to every function f satisfying the stated maximal
universal-lower-bound property, the conjecture follows.
